title: 25 years of stunning definition
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Ranked #78 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble portrait shows Messier 100, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Coma Berenices, taken with Wide Field Camera 3. Hubble has photographed this galaxy before, most famously in a pair of pictures made about a month apart, one before and one after the telescope's first servicing mission, flown in December a quarter of a century before this image was released.

Soon after launch, Hubble's pictures came back fuzzy, as though out of focus. Its main mirror, which works like a satellite dish gathering light to one focal point, had a flaw called spherical aberration, in which light hitting the mirror's rim did not meet at the same point as light from its middle.

Seven astronauts fixed this on that first servicing mission by fitting a device named COSTAR, which compensated for the flaw so the instruments could sharpen their images. The before-and-after pictures of M100 showed a big jump in quality. COSTAR stayed on board until Servicing Mission 4, and every later instrument had corrective optics built in.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal much more of the galaxy's faint structure than an eye could see.

explore: COSTAR stands for Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement. By the time it was removed, all of Hubble's original instruments had been swapped out. The newer M100 portrait shows how far the current generation of cameras has come compared with those Hubble carried at launch and just after the first repair.
